title_zh: 你无法看到一切——关于真相、信息与尽职调查的一则思考（Ted Seides 独白）
subtitle_zh: 由纪录片《You Can See Everything》引出：我们问出的问题，本身正在塑造我们得到的答案。
summary_zh: 本期 Capital Allocators 是 Ted Seides 的一则独白（WTT），由纪录片《You Can See Everything》（关于 Elizabeth Holmes，导演 Fielder）引出对真相、信息与尽职调查（due diligence）的反思。Seides 坦言，影片越是近距离接触 Holmes，观众对所谓基本真相（ground truth）反而越困惑——更多信息与透明度未必带来更多洞见。他借一位经营公开股票（public equity）投资公司的老友切入：业绩跑输大盘时，客户反复追问“你为什么会跑输、何时好转”，而基金经理明知无法预测，仍要演一出让人安心的戏。由此他提出核心质疑：会不会是尽调流程本身在塑造我们接收到的信息——我们的偏见影响问出的问题，问题又影响基金经理的答案，最终结论更多反映互动本身而非其真实投资方式。他指出配置方（allocator）想要的有时不是真相而是安心，双方散场都感觉好受些却没学到什么；善于观察者会更少盯着“说了什么”，而看基金经理在压力下的性情（temperament）、担当与一致性。他建议改问不一样的问题——“有哪些是你不知道的？什么情况会让你改变主意？你如何区分一个错误与一个不利的结果？”——因为这些更能揭示判断力，洞见也会随时间复利累积（compound）。是一则关于尽调认识论的精炼思辨。

turns.en: I curled up next to my wife in big, comfortable chairs at an AMC movie theater last weekend to watch the remarkable documentary you can see everything. I expected to learn more about Elizabeth Holmes, instead I left thinking about how we discover the truth.
turns.zh: 上周末，我和妻子窝在一家 AMC 影院宽大舒适的座椅里，去看了那部很出色的纪录片《You Can See Everything》。我本以为能更多地了解 Elizabeth Holmes，结果走出来时，满脑子想的却是我们究竟该如何去发现真相。

turns.en: The documentary offers a broad perspective on how we consume and interpret information. A great fielder implicitly poses important questions. How do we form beliefs? What do we know? And as Mark Twain said, what do we think we know that just ain't so? The irony of the movie title is that the more access fielder gained to Holmes, the more
turns.zh: 这部纪录片为我们如何接收和解读信息提供了一个很宽广的视角。这是部很棒的片子，Fielder 不动声色地抛出了几个重要问题：我们是怎么形成信念的？我们究竟知道些什么？还有，就像 Mark Twain 说的，有哪些我们自以为知道、其实压根不是那么回事的事？片名的反讽之处在于：Fielder 越是能近距离接触 Holmes，我们就越是……

turns.en: confused we become about the ground truth. Sometimes more information and more transparency do not lead to more insight. I left thinking more deeply about how we form perceptions and make decisions when the information in front of us is incomplete, biased, or wrong.
turns.zh: ……对那个所谓的基本真相（ground truth）感到困惑。有时候，更多的信息、更高的透明度，并不必然带来更多的洞见。走出影院时，我在更深地琢磨一个问题：当摆在我们面前的信息本身就不完整、有偏差、甚至是错误的时候，我们是怎么形成判断、又是怎么做决策的。

turns.en: The day before I had a long conversation with a close friend who runs a highly successful public equity firm. He had just returned from a week abroad visiting clients amid a period of underperformance. Each client asked some version of the same questions. Why did you underperform?
turns.zh: 就在前一天，我和一位老朋友聊了很久，他经营着一家非常成功的公开股票（public equity）投资公司。他刚从国外回来，那一周都在拜访客户，而当时正赶上业绩不及大盘的一段时期。每位客户问的都是同一个问题的不同版本：你为什么会跑输？

turns.en: Double change your fortunes and when will performance improve? He said to me, it was all bullshit. They know I don't know what will happen, but I have to perform to make them comfortable. It was exhausting and left me feeling empty. Behind closed doors I got access to a truth that rarely gets unearthed in a typical manager-allocator
turns.zh: 你打算怎么扭转局面、业绩什么时候才会好转？他跟我说，这一切都是扯淡。他们心里清楚我根本不知道接下来会发生什么，但我还是得演上一出，好让他们安心。这让他筋疲力尽，也让他觉得心里空落落的。关起门来，我听到了一个在典型的基金经理—配置方（manager-allocator）……

turns.en: conversation. I've been thinking about his comment ever since. Researchers make judgments about people. We visit their offices, meet their teams, dissect their portfolios, study their track records, and ask them to explain their investment process.
turns.zh: ……的对话里很少会被挖出来的一句真话。从那以后，我一直想着他说的这番话。我们做研究，要对着活生生的人下判断：我们去拜访他们的办公室，见他们的团队，逐一拆解他们的投资组合，研究他们过往的业绩记录（track record），还请他们讲解自己的投资流程。

turns.en: We assume that more meetings, more access, and more questions lead to a better understanding of the manager. But what if the process itself shapes the information we receive? Are biases influenced the questions we ask? Are questions influenced the answers managers give?
turns.zh: 我们默认，开得会越多、能接触到的越多、问的问题越多，就能把这位基金经理理解得越透。可万一，是这个流程本身在塑造我们接收到的信息呢？会不会是我们的偏见（biases）在影响我们问出的问题？又会不会是这些问题在影响基金经理给出的答案？

turns.en: And the conclusions we draw may tell us as much about the interaction as they do about how a manager actually invests. Turning back to my friend, when performance disappoints our careful assessment of process often gives way to a much simpler judgment of outcomes.
turns.zh: 而我们据此得出的结论，可能更多反映的是这场互动本身，而不是这位基金经理实际是怎么投资的。再回到我那位朋友身上：当业绩令人失望时，我们对投资流程那套审慎的评估，往往会让位于一个简单得多、只看结果的判断。

turns.en: As a result, we lead managers to telling us what we want to hear rather than what they know. Think about the questions we ask when a manager underperforms. Why did it happen? What have you learned? What will you do differently? And why should we expect better results?
turns.zh: 结果就是，我们其实是在诱导基金经理说出我们想听的话，而不是他们真正知道的东西。想想看，当一位基金经理跑输时，我们都会问些什么：为什么会这样？你从中学到了什么？接下来你会有什么不同的做法？我们又凭什么可以期待更好的结果？

turns.en: Taken at face value, these questions can carry an unreasonable expectation that a manager can explain the past with precision, identify what needs to change, and offer a positive outlook on an inherently uncertain future. This is particularly true in the public markets, where cause and effect carry a lot of noise
turns.zh: 如果照字面去理解，这些问题其实暗含了一种不太合理的期待：期待一位基金经理能精准地解释过去、能指出到底哪里需要改变，还能对一个本质上充满不确定性的未来给出乐观的展望。这一点在公开市场（public markets）里尤其如此，因为在那里，因果关系夹杂着大量的噪声（noise）——

turns.en: on any individual position. There's another uncomfortable possibility. Maybe allocators don't always want the truth as much as they want reassurance. Managers recognize this and respond accordingly. They emphasize their convictions, minimize their doubts, and present a plan.
turns.zh: ——落到任何单一持仓上都是如此。还有一种让人不太舒服的可能：也许配置方（allocators）想要的并不总是真相，而更多的是一份安心。基金经理们看得出来这一点，于是照着这个来回应：他们强调自己的信念，淡化自己的疑虑，再给出一套方案。

turns.en: The result is a conversation in which both sides may leave feeling better without either having learned very much. My friend knew he couldn't predict when his performance would improve. His clients probably knew that too, yet everyone participated in the ritual. He offered explanations and a path forward.
turns.zh: 结果就是，这样一场对话里，双方散场时可能都感觉好受了些，可谁其实都没学到多少东西。我那位朋友清楚，自己没法预测业绩什么时候会好转。他的客户大概心里也明白，但所有人都照例参与了这场仪式：他给出一套解释和一条往前走的路径，

turns.en: They listened, asked questions, and presumably left feeling a little bit better about staying invested. But did anyone leave the meeting with more insight? Perhaps there's more to these conversations than meets the eye. The questions asked when a manager underperforms may serve a purpose beyond their literal answers.
turns.zh: 他们听着、问着，散场时想必对继续持有这笔投资感觉踏实了那么一点点。可是，真有人带着更多洞见离开这场会面吗？也许，这些对话里藏着的东西比表面看到的要多。当一位基金经理跑输时，人们问出的那些问题，其作用可能远不止于它们字面上的答案。

turns.en: A student allocator might focus less on what a manager says than on how they behave under pressure. Testing a manager's temperament, accountability, consistency, and conviction at difficult times can offer insight irrespective of the answers the managers give.
turns.zh: 一位善于观察学习的配置方，或许会更少去盯着基金经理说了什么，而更多去看他们在压力之下是怎么表现的。在艰难时刻去检验一位基金经理的性情（temperament）、担当（accountability）、一致性（consistency）和信念（conviction），无论他们给出怎样的答案，都能带来洞见。

turns.en: In the repetitive exhaustion of what felt like playing defense, my friend may have missed the exception to the norm, an allocator playing the game within the game. You can see everything shows that seeing more doesn't necessarily mean understanding more.
turns.zh: 在那种一遍又一遍、像是在打防守战一样的疲惫里，我那位朋友可能错过了常规之外的例外——某个正在玩“游戏中游戏”（the game within the game）的配置方。《You Can See Everything》这部片子告诉我们：看到的更多，并不必然意味着理解得更深。

turns.en: The lesson isn't to stop asking hard questions or doing the painstaking work of due diligence. It's to recognize that the questions we ask can influence the answers we get. We might benefit from asking different questions, the deep in our understanding of what's really happening. Questions like, what don't you know?
turns.zh: 这里的教训，并不是让我们别再问那些尖锐的问题，或者不再去做那份费时费力的尽职调查（due diligence）。而是要认识到：我们问出的问题，会影响我们得到的答案。我们或许能从问一些不一样的问题中受益，从而更深地理解到底发生了什么。比如这样的问题：有哪些是你不知道的？

turns.en: What would cause you to change your mind? Where might your process fail? And how do you distinguish between a mistake and an unfavorable outcome? These questions reveal more about a manager's judgment, insights that can compound over time. We can't see everything. We can't know everything.
turns.zh: 什么情况会让你改变主意？你的投资流程可能在哪儿出问题？你又是怎么区分“一个错误”和“一个不利的结果”的？这些问题能更多地揭示出一位基金经理的判断力，而这些洞见会随着时间的推移不断复利累积（compound）。我们没法看到一切，也没法知道一切。

turns.en: And no matter how much work we do, we can't know what's going to happen where the motivations of everyone involved. But we can get better at recognizing how our own expectations shape the answers we receive. Perhaps the best way to get closer to the truth isn't to demand more information and
turns.zh: 而且，无论我们下多少功夫，都无从知道接下来会发生什么，也看不透每个参与方各自的动机。但我们可以在一件事上做得更好：认清我们自己的期待，是如何在塑造我们收到的答案的。也许，离真相更近的最好办法，并不是去索要更多的信息、

turns.en: more certainty, but to make it easier for others to reveal their uncertainty. Thanks for listening to the show. If you like what you heard, hop on our website at capitalislecators.com where you can access past shows, join our mailing list, and sign up for premium content. Have a good one and see you next time.
turns.zh: 更多的确定性，而是让别人更容易把自己不确定的那一面袒露出来。感谢收听本期节目。如果你喜欢今天听到的内容，欢迎上我们的网站 capitalallocators.com，在那里你可以回听往期节目、订阅我们的邮件列表，还能注册获取付费内容。祝你愉快，我们下期再见。
